utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. This is case number IT-04-81, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can I take this opportunity just to welcome the parties to this Status Conference and ask for the appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Mark Harmon and Evangelos Thomas appearing on behalf of the Prosecution; we're assisted by Carmela Javier the case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. For the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CASTLE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour, Jim Castle appearing on behalf of Momcilo Perisic, whose appearance has been waived for today. Also appearing here today is Novak Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Just to remind the parties that by order dated the 26th of March, 2008, I was assigned as the Pre-Trial Judge in this case. As you have said, Mr. Castle, we note that the accused is on provisional release and he has waived his right to attend today's conference. If I'm not mistaken I think I read in the filing that waived that right an indication that he may be on a videolink conference, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. CASTLE
utterances.text: Yes, he would be available by videolink, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But he's not going to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. CASTLE
utterances.text: He's not appearing by videolink. It's just if there is a matter that we need to address with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'm sorry, Mr. Castle, that causes me a little bit of confusion. You say if there is a matter that we need to be discussed with him. Are you saying the videolink is ready to be switched on if need be?

utterances.speaker: MR. CASTLE
utterances.text: That is my understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Castle, I'm advised to the contrary, that a request had been for a teleconference link and that no arrangements have been made for a videolink to be in place should one be necessary. So it does seem as if we are going to have to dispense with communicating with the accused at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. CASTLE
utterances.text: I stand corrected. I also do not anticipate there being a need to have any conversations with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much, Mr. Castle. While we're talking about the accused being on provisional release, Mr. Castle, may I ask you to be exercising in your mind during this conference and when we come to talk about the trial dates just think about the last request that you filed -- that was filed on behalf of the accused for changing of conditions of release, for visitation -- the dates of visitations. You don't have to answer me right now. Okay. Can we just move on to the next item, which is the reasons for this Status Conference. The last Status Conference was held on the 15th of January, 2008, and pursuant to Rule 65 bis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, a Status Conference shall be convened within 120 days of the last Status Conference in order to organize an exchange between the parties, to ensure exchanges between the parties solely and to ensure the expeditious preparation for trial and to allow the accused to raise issues in relation to the case. Are there any issues that maybe you may want to raise with respect to the health of the accused, Mr. Castle?

utterances.speaker: MR. CASTLE
utterances.text: Not at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Not at this time. To your knowledge he is in good health?

utterances.speaker: MR. CASTLE
utterances.text: Yes, he is in good health to this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Harmon, I don't think you have any contribution to make on that position?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We have nothing to say on that matter, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Can we then move on to pending motions. There is a motion on provisional release that was filed on the 2nd of May, 2008, by the Defence requesting alteration of the conditions of provisional release. The Chamber would like to know whether the Prosecution intends to respond to this motion, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We do not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You do not. Thank you very much. In that event, then, an order will be issued in due course and again when we discuss the dates we'll try to tie that with this motion. Okay. Thank you very much. Then the next item was -- well, the next motion was on adjudicated facts. On 6th February 2007, the Prosecution filed the Prosecution's motion for judicial notice of adjudicated facts concerning Sarajevo, and in that motion it requests the Trial Chamber pursuant to Rule 94 bis of the Rules to take judicial notice of 314 facts which have been adjudicated in the Galic case. And the Defence filed two responses, and this motion is currently pending, but on the 23rd of May, 2007, the Pre-Trial Judge indicated that the motion for admission of adjudicated facts should be determined by the Trial Chamber that will hear the case. The Trial Chamber has still not been constituted, but if I might give my personal inclination, Mr. Harmon, I would prefer adjudicated facts to be agreed to the extent possible. Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, of course that would be my preference as well, but to date counsel and I have had discussions about certain facts that relate to the indictment, particularly Srebrenica. There have been agreed-upon facts in respect of Srebrenica. The discussions over a year ago stopped in respect of agreements of the parties in terms of facts. Now, that's not to say that we will not reach further agreements in the meantime, but for purposes of trial planning, obviously it's in the interests -- in our interests to know what is going to be adjudicated and what is not. If one examines the motion that we filed in February of 2007, we, you will see, Your Honour, and the Trial Chamber will see, that there are nine scheduled incidents that -- for which we ask that the Court make a decision. Obviously the effect of reaching a decision on that will impact on our ability to plan and could well shorten the trial. I don't have at my disposal how many witnesses would be eliminated with this, but it seems to me, Your Honour, that given that we have had over a year where we have not been able to -- it's not that we haven't been able to reach agreements, we haven't had those conversations. And I'm told by Mr. Castle and Mr. Simic that the possibility exists, but that's only a possibility. And for our purposes, it's very, very important that this motion be decided before the trial commences. Obviously if we are able to reach agreements before the commencement of trial, we'll bring that immediately to the Court's attention. But I think I will strive, I can make an undertaking to Your Honour, I'll strive to participate in such discussions constructively. I'm anxious to reach agreements, but obviously I'm limited in what I can do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I really would like to encourage the parties to continue negotiating. I personally have a philosophical problem with admitting adjudicated facts. In another case when this accused in that case was not represented in that case and we don't even know whoever was being tried in that case was trying to implicate this accused, we really don't know. And that's why I'm encouraging the parties to try as far as it is possible to reach agreement, particularly because the Defence is objecting to those -- to the admission of those adjudicated facts, you know. So it makes it a little difficult to go over that philosophical problem. Okay. Do you have anything to add on to that, Mr. Castle?

utterances.speaker: MR. CASTLE
utterances.text: The only thing that I would add is to explain to the Court what the impediment to further agreements is so that we all understand what the problem is. When the Defence first engaged in this process, we agreed to a number of the -- the admission of a number of documents, a number of statements, then we proceeded to agree to a certain facts that were related to the Srebrenica portion of the indictment. It was our hope that with those agreements there would be a concomitant reduction in the exposure our client faced, that there would be some reduction on the part of the Prosecution or that a 73 bis decision would reduce the number of counts that our client faced at trial, but that didn't happen. And that's what stopped the negotiation because the negotiation was a one-way street of the Defence agreeing to facts that literally would lean towards his conviction without anything in return. I have to let the Court know, we're not trying to stall for the purposes of stalling, it's just that negotiations normally have to take place in a situation where there is give and take. And I won't say Mr. Harmon has been completely unreasonable, I'm not saying that. Part of the problem is we don't sit down and talk because we're in different countries and different locations. I'm hopeful when we're -- our Defence team is here and we're able to sit down, Mr. Harmon, perhaps his wisdom can prevail upon us. But that essentially is what our problem is here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I hear what you say, but let me make these two comments. It seems to me what you consider as a reason for agreeing facts is somewhat slightly different from what is normally expected. I think you agree a fact because you believe that fact is fact, not because you are plea bargaining. But when you say you want a two-way street it seems to me that you are plea bargaining. The next point I would like to make is that we are not yet at the stage of 73 bis. We are still getting there, and most probably the Prosecution is going to be asked to reduce its indictment one way or the other when we get to that stage. So I would try and encourage you to look at the facts and see whether this is a fact that you can accept that has taken place, it exists, and is there a need really to call a witness to establish it. You know, I think that should be the consideration. Thank you very much. Can we leave that point on the understanding that the parties will carry on negotiating and trying to find each other on the adjudicated facts?

utterances.speaker: MR. CASTLE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, that's certainly acceptable. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My apologies, I'm being advised that, in fact, the 73 bis decision has been taken on the 15th of May, 2007. You are aware of that, Mr. Castle?

utterances.speaker: MR. CASTLE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You didn't hear. I was just apologising for misstating the situation. I thought we hadn't reached the 73 bis stage yet, but I'm advised that that decision was taken on the 15th of May, 2007.

utterances.speaker: MR. CASTLE
utterances.text: That's my understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And that in fact some -- either incidents or charges were cut out of the indictment. Can you confirm that, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The indictment was reduced as per the order of the Pre-Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: To which then I would just say, Mr. Castle, that if indeed you are looking for something in return you have heard that bit through that 73 bis decision already.

utterances.speaker: MR. CASTLE
utterances.text: The only thing I would note is that actually there was nothing cut out of the indictment at all. The only thing that was cut was that Mr. Harmon had been requested to bring in other bad acts or other acts that were not charged in the indictment, and the trial was reduced in the eyes of the Court by saying, We're issuing a ruling that absent some compelling showing of relevancy that the Prosecution would not be allowed to bring in evidence of these other acts. So not a single count was eliminated in that -- I think that's a fair statement of the 73 bis decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No count was eliminated, but were incidents within counts cut out?

utterances.speaker: MR. CASTLE
utterances.text: No incidents within counts were cut out. Only -- to give the Court an idea, there was a number of witnesses that were endorsed by the Prosecution which related to other events, namely, many in the Sarajevo region. And the Court reviewed the number of witnesses as being indicative of the scope of the trial and attempted to reduce the scope of the trial by a third and did so not through reducing counts or crime bases, but by issuing an order indicating that absent compelling reasons that the Prosecution would not be able to call those additional witnesses that related to other events that were not charged in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Harmon, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: There were a number of schedules in particular in respect of Sarajevo I think there are 21 scheduled incidents. In the documents that we had filed with the Court, we sought to lead other acts in addition to the 21 scheduled incidents and we were instructed by the Trial Chamber that we would not be able to do so unless we had a compelling reason and we sought leave of the Court to do so. So as a result of that we were able to reduce, per the Court instruction, the scope of the evidence, the volume of evidence that was being led. It did not result in the elimination of a single count because the counts stayed whether or not there was other act evidence. So in terms of what was reduced and what we were instructed to do we have complied fully with the Court's order. We have not to date filed any motions seeking leave of the Court to admit other act evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This other evidence is the evidence that was outside the 21 scheduled incidents?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. For example, Your Honour, what came -- one issue is we have 21 scheduled incidents of shelling and sniping. Now, we allege in the indictment there's a campaign of fire directed at civilian targets, both shelling and sniping. To establish the campaign, we sought to introduce additional evidence that would support the 21 acts. And the Court said to us in clear terms, You are at this point in time precluded, but not forever, from introducing that other act evidence. If you have a compelling need to do so, you make an application to the Trial Chamber. So the elimination of the other act evidence did not result in the elimination of any counts in the indictment, but it resulted in a reduction in the trial that the Pre-Trial Chamber then was facing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I speak subject to correction, but the rule on reduction of the case does not necessarily require reduction by way of cutting out counts, it just wants you to reduce the scope of the case. To show -- the idea is to shorten the estimated length of the examination-in-chief for some witnesses, and the Court may order that the number of witnesses the Prosecutor may call and the number -- the time available to the Prosecutor for presenting evidence. It doesn't call upon the Prosecution to cut out counts as I understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We have the same understanding, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. So -- and you say you've complied with the 73 bis decision of the Pre-Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We did, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And to that extent, Mr. Castle, you have heard the quid pro quo that you are looking for. Okay. Just as a final parting note on this, I remind the parties once again to please try to reach agreement on those adjudicated facts. Then there is the motions pursuant to Rules 92 bis, ter, and quater. Again, at the Status Conference of the 15th of January this year it was anticipated that the decision of these motions would be taken in due course by the Trial Chamber that will hear the case. Again, I'm also inclined to say that matter of admitting evidence is a matter for a Trial Chamber not just a Pre-Trial Judge. I don't know whether the parties have anything to say, Mr. Harmon, on the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I have nothing to add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Castle?

utterances.speaker: MR. CASTLE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: All I can say is we will try to reach a decision as soon as the Trial Chamber is constituted, and give a decision. And there was a motions to amend exhibit and witness lists. I think two motions are pending before the Chamber regarding the 65 ter exhibit list, being the Prosecution motion for leave to file a third supplement Rule 65 ter list with annex A filed confidentially on the 28th of February, 2008, and Prosecution motion for leave to file a fourth supplemental Rule 65 ter exhibit list with annex A filed confidentially on the 28th of March, 2008. No response has been filed by the Defence for the motion of the 28th of February, while a response for the motion of the 28th of March has been -- was filed on the 10th of April. Mr. Castle, is there -- does that response suffice for both motions or does the --

utterances.speaker: MR. CASTLE
utterances.text: The response only dealt with the second of the motions. The first one we did not have objections to, so we did not file a response to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That clears the point. Okay. Just out of an abundance of caution, could we move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The next item relates to disclosure issues. It is the Chamber's general impression that the Prosecution has complied with all its obligations pursuant to Rule 66(A). Are you able to confirm that, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, we believe we have, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But for the summaries of the French witness statements?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, obviously with that exception.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's right. So once that -- you confirm that once that has been disclosed, those have been disclosed, you will have complied.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And one additional. We have a previous Court order that permits us to disclose the witness statements, three witness statements, to the Defence 30 days before the commencement of trial, so that's another category of statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's right. Sure. Okay. Thank you very much. Mr. Castle, any comment?

utterances.speaker: MR. CASTLE
utterances.text: No comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No comment. Good. Then the Rule 68 obligations, that's an ongoing obligation and I would imagine that the Prosecutor is continuously disclosing to the Defence whatever needs to be disclosed. Are you happy in that line of disclosure, Mr. Castle, so far?

utterances.speaker: MR. CASTLE
utterances.text: We're not aware of any exculpatory material that has not been turned over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That is very helpful to know. And let's then move on to Rule 66(B). Now, according to the order establishing a work-plan issued on the 11th of October, 2006, the Prosecution should have complied with all its obligations under this rule at this point I would imagine.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. And on the 31st of October, 2007, the Prosecution filed a report on outstanding translations in this case pursuant to an order of the Chamber issued on the 19th of September, 2007. In that report the Prosecution indicated approximately 9.000 pages of documents remaining to be translated, and the Prosecution indicated that that translation would be complete by the 31st of January, 2008, and that if it was not complete the Prosecution would give a report. No report has been received. Can this Chamber assume that that -- those translations are complete?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Those translations I believe are complete. They were complete by the dead-line imposed by the Trial Chamber. The other issue, however, I wanted to alert Your Honour to is that we have had ongoing litigation with Serbia to get additional documents that we deem relevant to this Prosecution. And the Court can see as a result of the filing of 54 bis motions that we've had some difficulties in getting full compliance. The motions before Your Honour on 54 bis are not the first set of 54 bis motions that we have filed. What does that mean? In terms of the production of documents, some of which are voluminous to us, when we finally get them they are not translated for us. So we are faced with, again, a problem with translation of those relevant documents. We have taken extraordinary measures to ensure that we can get those documents translated as soon as possible, and then when they get translated their benefit to me as the Prosecutor and we disclose them to the Defence immediately. So we've also -- we've also undertaken a regime that when I get documents that I think are relevant in B/C/S I give them to the Defence before I get them translated. Because on the Defence team the Defence has people who read the language and can study the documents. So in one sense they're often better advanced than I am in terms of understanding the content of those documents, but in order to ameliorate any issues that could be raised by any issues that might affect the ability of this trial to go forward, we've taken positive steps to disclose them immediately to the Defence in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's where we are in terms of translations, Your Honour. I don't want the Court to be misled believing that all the translations that are relevant to this case have been completed. The 9.000 pages were on time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand that very much, Mr. Harmon. The question really related to the 9.000 pages. You have just told me those have been translated, those have been disclosed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Obviously any material that is not currently in your possession or that has recently come into your possession and still needs to be translated still has to be translated before it can be disclosed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's quite understandable. And I'm sure you understand that too, Mr. Castle.

utterances.speaker: MR. CASTLE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's just a practical notion.

utterances.speaker: MR. CASTLE
utterances.text: Yes, and just for the Court to know, I have no evidence that the Prosecution has been dilatory in an attempt to get documents translated, but other cases in this Tribunal have absorbed resources that would ordinarily be available to have items translated. We have been working with the Prosecution to identify items that we need translated and the ones that we have a high priority on, and I belive that process is continuing to work well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Agreed matters of law or facts. On the 1st of May the parties files a joint submission on agreed matters of law. On the 1st of June, 2007, again the parties filed a joint submission on agreed facts. All agreed facts relate to the crimes allegedly committed in Srebrenica. These agreed facts are recorded by the Chamber pursuant to Rule 65 ter (H) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence and the Chamber encourages the parties to further develop the area of agreed facts to the extent possible. Is there any comment that you would like to make on that item, Mr. Harmon, on agreed facts?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Nothing. Mr. Castle?

utterances.speaker: MR. CASTLE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, we'll just keep the Court informed as we go along if there's any changes in that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Again, like with adjudicated facts, the Chamber still encourages the parties to agree as many facts as possible. That will help to shorten the trial also. Let's deal with the little difficult question of the anticipated length of the trial and the trial date. On the 23rd of May, 2007, the Prosecution estimated that if none of its Rule 92 bis motions are granted, and assuming that there is a sitting of five days a week in the normal course of business with very few interruptions, the entire length of the trial will last a year and a half. You confirm that, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just amplify that. Yes, I confirm that I said that on the 23rd of May and that has been raised in subsequent conferences, in 65 ter conferences, and I believe the last Status Conference as well. Obviously both parties want to reduce this trial. We --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's a good start.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, I think we genuinely -- the parties have been willing to work together, have been unable to do so because there's a vast distance between Denver, Colorado, and The Hague. We're now here and when Mr. Castle and his team get installed, I think we will work hard to try to reduce this in a more understandable systematic way than we have been able to do so far. The 15 months obviously is an estimate. I was asked on the 23rd of May to speculate, and it's very, very difficult to speculate to -- when you have literally hundreds of motions that are outstanding and have not been decided. So that -- I want to reinforce, Your Honour, that this was a best guess possible. We will try to make it shorter than that, but I can also envision if there are no agreements and there are -- we have to establish crime base material that I think is not really contested, but if we have to go through the exercise then it will take some time and it may well go over 15 months. That was my best estimate then. It remains my best estimate. I think we'll come in shorter than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, can I try and tie your hands behind your back a little bit. You started very well by saying it is everybody's intention and wish to shorten the case. You end up by saying it might go little beyond by 15 months. I want to cut that part out. That's where I want to tie your hands. And I do by saying the best estimate you were asked to make, and as I read out that little paragraph, was made on the assumption that none of your 92 bis and ter and quater motions were granted and that therefore your entire case was going to be viva voce. In other words, it was on a worst-case-scenario basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I accept that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I accept that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So if it wasn't a worst-case scenario basis, I don't anticipate going beyond your worst case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, when I was asked this question yesterday by the Senior Legal Officer, I went back and read my comments and I said that the trial would last with all those conditions 15 months. But I was -- what I was trying to say and I didn't say it well enough was, the Prosecution case in chief would last 15 months. I can't speak for the Defence case and how long that is going to take. Whether that is incorporated in -- whether the Trial Chamber understands the Defence case to be rolled into the 15-month estimate certainly wasn't by intention because I can't speak for the Defence. I stand by a 15-month estimate outside for the Prosecution's case in chief, but the length of the trial I can't speak for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's a major departure, Mr. Harmon, I must say.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may reiterate to you the last bit of the sentence that I said to you, the estimate was that the entire length of the trial will last a year and a half. Now, I'm not suggesting I'm quoting you. I'm suggesting this is the impression that this Chamber is left with, that is the entire length of the trial. Now, if you say 18 months for just the Prosecution phase, now are you saying that on a one-to-one basis we are likely to be here for three years?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I hope not, Your Honour. I've been through one trial that lasted 32 months, and I don't care to repeat it. What I was trying to say and what I can control in my estimate is the Prosecution's case. Mr. Castle and I never discussed at that point in time how long the Defence case would last. I don't know how long the Defence case is going to last, and I don't think it would be, quite honestly, something you would want to rely on me estimating the length of the Defence case. I can tell you that 15 months is -- was a -- my best guess under those conditions for the Prosecution case. That's what I can say, and I think it will come in, assuming we reach some agreements, I think it will come in shorter than that. We will endeavour to make it come in shorter than that. But perhaps, you know, the -- I shouldn't be speaking for the Defence in terms of how long their case will last because that's not -- I'm not in a position to do so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's true, and I would imagine that the Defence usually does make that estimate at the opening of the Defence case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm sure they do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Not at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So there's no point in trying to even engage Mr. Castle on the point, on an estimation of their case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Of course --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We can't do that at this stage. Anyway, let's sort of go through the implications of what you are saying. When one calculates the length of time one bears in mind that we have a 52-week year. We have various recesses and adjournments during the year that effectively bring about a working year to something like 41 weeks. And 41 weeks on the assumption that you sit five days at 3.5 hours a day brings you to something like 720 hours in a year. I see you shaking your head.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] As you're talking, Your Honour, I'm doing some calculations myself. No disrespect intended.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Not a problem, not a problem. Indeed my calculations are also a rough calculations, and I would appreciate being corrected as I go along. Okay. Now, the Chamber is also aware that the estimated time is still subject to further revision in light of the pending motions. Anyway, based on the revised witness list filed by the Prosecution on the 28th of June, 2007, and the required hours indicated therein, the Chamber has calculated an estimated time of 907 hours for the direct examination of Prosecution witnesses. It is a striking difference and -- considering that the Prosecution took steps in accordance with the Chamber's Rule 73 bis decision to reduce the estimated time of 950 hours by 169 hours in relation to the Sarajevo component of the case. And then I think it should also be borne in mind that the same amount of time for cross-examination and perhaps something like 25 per cent for re-direct, questions from the Bench, et cetera, should be added to that estimated time. That overall number would then come to something like 2.040 hours, which corresponds to nearly three years only -- for the Prosecution case only.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I can assure you, Your Honour, we don't intend to lead evidence for three years in our case, and we will find ways to reduce three years so all the parties are satisfied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Can I then suggest or make a contribution to what you are going to do to cut down to make sure that we are not here for three years. If we try to ask the Prosecution to stay within nine months to complete its case, which would give you 540 hours for the Prosecution phase; in other words, something like 220 hours for direct, 220 for cross, 100 for re-examination, something like that roughly. How would that work out?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I would have to study those figures, Your Honour, in light of our witness list and other matters, but I will certainly study that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: -- very carefully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- do and the Prosecution is invited and once studied that to file a witness list in accordance with those indications and how they've studied them. Would you like to tie yourself to a time-line on the witness list? I'm being kind. I don't -- I'm not imposing the time-line. I want you to tie yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: May I get back to you on that, Your Honour. I just don't know the schedules of my team at this point. I know I'm going to be away a period of time in the next two weeks and I need to find out what other peoples' schedules are. If I can get back to you on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How soon can you get back?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Just think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Let me throw a two-week timeline to you which you can put into equation as you talk to your staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me just look at the calendar I have in front of me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CASTLE
utterances.text: Your Honour, if it's possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Castle.

utterances.speaker: MR. CASTLE
utterances.text: I don't want to be a pessimist, but if one's to look at the indictment it is enormous. We have I think it's 32 endorsed experts in the case, almost 10.000 exhibits that include almost 100.000 pages of material. The constituent cases that make up parts of this each took in excess of two years to try, the constituent parts, the Sarajevo, each part. On top of that we're dealing with the political structure and the military structure of three different armies and the inter-relationships of those three armies. We're going to try to the best of our ability to cut down on a lot of the crime base evidence, but -- and I have never had a trial here before so guessing the estimate is a pure guess. But I don't know how this trial's going to be shorter, the people that were the subordinates, the alleged subordinates, of my client's trials. I don't know how that's possible when the linkage evidence is going to be more difficult to prove. I just want to let the Court know that I fear that despite everyone's best efforts that the trial may last longer than we anticipate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's true. We do factor that in, Mr. Castle. All what we are doing here is our best guesstimate. It's not even an estimate, it's just a guesstimate, and it's subject to change as we go along.

utterances.speaker: MR. CASTLE
utterances.text: The only reason I bring that up and it's perhaps our hope is that 73 bis doesn't indicate that the Court only gets one opportunity to reduce the size of the Prosecution's case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. CASTLE
utterances.text: I think it can be used a number of times in the case as need be. And so with that in mind we have no other comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Your comment is noted. Thank you, Mr. Castle. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could inform the Court by the 20th of May, if that would be acceptable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That is essentially two weeks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. 20th of May. Thank you. We'll note that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, I suppose you referred to hundreds of motions outstanding. Do I understand by that to mean -- to refer to the 92 bis, ter, quater and -- motions and the witnesses individually?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. I referred to approximately 44, 92 bis decisions that have to be taken in respect of individual witnesses where we have attached to the 92 bis motion a schedule identifying the parts of the written evidence for which we seek admission; and the exhibits in respect of 92 ter, there's approximately 80 -- one motion but a schedule with 85 individual decisions that have to be taken; 92 quater there are approximately ten separate motions before the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We understand that. I was just getting scared that there may be hundreds of motions that the Court is not aware of. Now I understand what you are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. CASTLE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Castle. As for the date of trial, can we start by saying that the parties should perhaps try to be ready to start the trial in earnest shortly after the summer recess. The Chamber considers holding a Pre-Trial Conference and opening statements just before the summer recess if it's possible. And depending on what the parties -- how the parties feel about this, the Chamber would like to propose Monday, the 21st of July, 2008, for Pre-Trial Conference; and Thursday, the 25th of July, 2008, for opening statements. There might -- and while we are on that, Mr. Castle, if I may just find out at what stage of the trial would the Defence like to make an opening statement, if they do wish to make a statement at all?

utterances.speaker: MR. CASTLE
utterances.text: We've been talking about that and we have not yet made a decision. In the event that we did wish to avail ourselves of an opening statement, we do not anticipate it to be an extremely long one. I guess that's a loaded term, but I'm talking not -- I mean, half a day maximum. But we have not made a decision fully on that yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Is there a possibility that you can -- that you might make a decision in favour of making an opening statement before the opening of the Prosecution trial -- case?

utterances.speaker: MR. CASTLE
utterances.text: There is a possibility of that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: There is a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. CASTLE
utterances.text: I know that's not normally the practice of Defence here, but sometimes I'm less Orthodox.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You -- it's up to you. Okay. The reason I ask this question is because just in case the opening statement of the Prosecution takes the entire 25th of July, then we should be able to provide the 26th for you to make your opening statement. Otherwise, if you want to make it at the opening of the Defence case, that's your choice.

utterances.speaker: MR. CASTLE
utterances.text: That's alright, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you suggest that we make provision for the 26th of July?

utterances.speaker: MR. CASTLE
utterances.text: I would suggest so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We will do that. Thank you so much. But again, I understand from the parties that you agree to this date so that a Scheduling Order can be issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's agreeable, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that agreeable?

utterances.speaker: MR. CASTLE
utterances.text: That's agreeable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, the start of the actual trial, that's what we need to talk about and then bear in mind the defendant's -- the accused's motion. The Chamber at this stage is not able to give clear guidance for the simple reason that there are still the Delic commitments. And the anticipation, however, is that within a month or so after the recess we should be able to start full blast with the trial; that is, end of August/beginning of September. It's a rough indication. We will re-visit that in due course as we see the progress in the other case. Is that reasonable and agreeable to the parties. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: May I just clarify something, Your Honour, just so it's clear in my own mind. The recess I think will end in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Third week of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: -- August?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: August -- I'll tell you --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: 20 -- it may be the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'll tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you. It may be August 15th, Your Honour, is when the recess ends.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's what I'm told, it ends on the 15th. So.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, yes. You are right, it ends on the 15th.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. I'm clear now reading Your Honour's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: -- comments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So we say we could start trial end of August/beginning of September somewhere in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. That's clear. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's a rough estimate. That said, are you looking at the visitations of the accused to the -- do you need a private session for this?

utterances.speaker: MR. CASTLE
utterances.text: No we don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Your Honour, may I just return to the date of the opening statement because looking at the calendar, it's been brought to my attention that the 26th is a Saturday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The 25th --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The 25th is a Friday. In the court schedule the Prosecution opening statement on the 25th of July and the Defence for the 26th, but the 26th is a Saturday. So ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you for bringing that to our attention, Mr. Harmon. Could we shift then the opening statements by the Prosecution to Thursday, the 24th, and then any possible Defence opening on Friday, the 25th? Is that okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. CASTLE
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I must also make a note. Thank you so much. That said, Mr. Castle, do you find any need to change the dates or to do anything to that motion?

utterances.speaker: MR. CASTLE
utterances.text: Yes. Our request for alterations in the terms of provisional release asked for three separate periods of time, the third of which took place in July. We would withdraw the request for that third period at this point in time. If something changes and we're not going to be in court, we'll re-raise it by a separate motion. We also would anticipate filing a motion allowing our client to return to his country by the summer break, but we'll do that by separate motion also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Castle. Are there any issues that the parties would like to raise? That brings me to the send of the formal agenda by the Chamber. Is there anything that the parties would like to raise. Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Nothing. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Castle.

utterances.speaker: MR. CASTLE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, just briefly. The -- we're on the verge of trial and one of the considerations always is how prepared the sides are for trial. And I need to make a record on what our situation is. Now, I'm not asking for an extension of the trial date, but I think that we need to put on the record what our situation is. Our client is facing a very, very large indictment, three different years of war, three different locations, three different armies, it's part of the Slobodan Milosevic case, it's portions of the Galic case, the Krstic case, the Martic case, all rolled into one. It's I believe the second-largest indictment in terms of scope that's been at this Tribunal. We're the only Defence team because Mr. Milosevic didn't choose -- he chose to represent himself, we're the only Defence team that has been found in that position. We have been saddled with the exact same budget that Defence counsel have in multiple Defence cases have and can share multiple versions of that same budget and add them on to each other to defend their clients. We're faced against a Prosecution team that will have a number of lawyers on their team, and they have on-staff military experts that are on staff and have been working on this case or portions of this case over a decade. That's what we're faced with. In addition, myself and co-counsel for the last year have not been compensated for our work. We have been able to compensate our staff but not the lawyers for any of our work. So we're in that position. So to say that we're ready for this trial would not be accurate, we're not, but each day that the trial doesn't happen the disparity and the gap and the inequality of arms gets -- becomes greater because the Prosecution continues to work, which I would expect them to do; and I don't fault them for doing, but we can't. And so we wish to go to trial starting in July because it's our best moment to because if we wait any longer the gap will be larger and larger and larger. And I bring this to this Court's attention. I have to the prior Court and we have made numerous requests to expand it, but there is an element of unfairness that will pervade this case based upon the fact that we're not going to be on equal footing. And that is how we will start the case. And anything this Court can do to encourage the registry to provide additional resources I think will not only have the benefit of providing the defendant with a fair trial, but frankly will also make the trial go smoother and lead to more agreements and more resolutions. I bring that to this Court for its consideration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me hone in on your request to the Court to encourage the registry to provide additional resources. Do I understand you to say that -- you're talking of monetary resources?

utterances.speaker: MR. CASTLE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I may be wrong, but from the little experience I have on that issue it doesn't seem as if we, the Court, is able to do anything unless and until something's placed before the Court on that matter. Usually that's a matter that Defence counsel negotiates with OLAD and what have you, and if Defence counsel feels dug-in by OLAD then you put your case before us and we look at it -- I don't even know the rating of the case. I haven't heard anything about this case, whether it's level A, B, or C, or -- what do they call them? 1, 2, or 3, I can't even remember now. It looks like there are three levels. I don't even know what level of complexity this case enjoys with OLAD. And I would imagine what you have said to us in terms of the enormity of the case, the complexity of the case, the scope of the case, those are all points in motivation for reconsideration by OLAD for that I suggest to you, you put before the Court. And I can suggest to you if and when you are still not satisfied, only then you can come before us. But there is no way without a -- at least a written motion that the Court would intervene.

utterances.speaker: MR. CASTLE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and I wasn't actually asking for any specific relief at this time. I just wanted the Court to know before we began this venture that there may be times when we may need delays or more time. And I did not want our acceptance of the trial date to be viewed as an affirmation that we are as prepared as we should be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- no, I understand. Thank you very much. Is that all that you wanted to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. CASTLE
utterances.text: That is all, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you have any comment to make on that, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I do not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you still have nothing to raise from the Prosecution's side?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Nothing, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In that event, that brings us to the conclusion of today's Status Conference. The court stands adjourned until further notice. Court adjourned.
